supporting: the distinction between deliverables, activities, and organizational charts

claims.claim: A work breakdown structure is a hierarchical, deliverable-oriented decomposition of the total project scope into smaller components.
The 100-percent concept means that child elements together represent all of their parent element's included work, without omitting work or adding work beyond the parent.

A work package is a lowest-level WBS component used as a manageable point for planning and relating work to supporting information; an activity schedule can be developed from the decomposition but is not the WBS itself.
A WBS can help make scope visible and provide a common structure for considering schedule, cost, risk, and performance information, but it does not guarantee those outcomes.
The useful degree of decomposition depends on the project and should be sufficient to manage the work without treating one level count or format as universal.
A WBS is not an organizational chart or a chronological to-do list: it organizes the scope by deliverable components before a schedule sequences activities.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The sources use WBS in government program, cost-estimating, and PMI practice contexts that can involve far more formal controls than a small classroom project.
positions: GAO explains WBS as part of detailed program cost and schedule practice.
PMI describes general decomposition principles and recognizes that the appropriate detail depends on the work.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches WBS as an adaptable analytical structure. It does not prescribe a mandatory template, number of levels, coding scheme, authority, or reporting process.

unsupportedExistingClaims: A generic draft could mistake a WBS for a schedule, a staffing chart, or a promise that planning will prevent all omissions or delays.
correctionsNeeded: Uses original prose and an original neighborhood-event example rather than reproducing source illustrations or templates.
States the 100-percent concept as a coverage and boundary check, not as a prediction of effort, cost, or success.
Separates deliverable decomposition from later activity sequencing and organizational assignment.
rightsIssues: PMI material was read live and is treated as REFERENCE_ONLY; no source prose, diagrams, templates, or coding schemes are reproduced.
GAO guides were read live and are U.S. government publications; the lesson uses original prose and reproduces no tables or figures.

questionKeyCheck.method: Read every saved prompt, all four options, correctIndex, explanation, and sourceIds after writing.
questionKeyCheck.result: Exactly five four-option questions. Keys cover A through D, no position occurs more than twice, and the bank includes recall, application, and analysis.

sourceRecords.title: Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide: Best Practices for Developing and Managing Program Costs (GAO-20-195G)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live, especially chapter 7. Supports product-oriented, hierarchical WBS concepts, parent-child coverage, work packages, and links to scheduling. The lesson does not reproduce guide figures or federal procedures.

sourceRecords.title: Developing and elaborating effective work breakdown structures
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. Supports deliverable orientation, hierarchical decomposition, the 100-percent concept, and context-dependent level of detail. An authored PMI paper; original prose only.

sourceRecords.title: Schedule Assessment Guide: Best Practices for Project Schedules (GAO-16-89G)
sourceRecords.notes: Official GAO guide checked live, especially Best Practices 6 and 7. Supports longest-duration critical path, earliest completion, total float, zero-float conditions, and cautions about logic, duration, status, and constraint defects. Original prose and hypothetical arithmetic only.
